messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Model
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 41

She is sixty-six now, a North American woman who still works as a model, though the work has changed with age—more catalog shoots, beauty campaigns, the occasional advertisement for jewelry or skin care. For most of her life she has moved through studios with the practiced ease of someone used to being looked at. She knows how to hold still under bright lights, how to take direction, how to make her face appear calm even when she is tired. She says this as if it explains something important about what happened later: she has spent decades learning to control what other people can see.

The event she returns to begins on an ordinary weekday afternoon three years ago. She has finished a fitting downtown and is driving herself home, garment bag folded across the back seat, still wearing more makeup than usual. Traffic is slow but moving. At an intersection she glances down for what she insists is only a second—her phone lights up with a message from a client asking about availability for a reshoot. When she looks up, the crosswalk is no longer empty. A cyclist has moved into her path. She brakes hard, hears the sound before she understands it, a sickening impact she says she still feels in her teeth. The woman on the bicycle is thrown sideways and lands badly. People are suddenly everywhere. Someone is shouting for an ambulance. She is out of the car, kneeling on the pavement, saying “I’m sorry” over and over to a stranger whose leg is bent in a way that should not be possible.

She learns later that the cyclist survives but suffers multiple fractures and a long recovery. No one dies, and she repeats that fact often, as if it ought to settle the matter. Instead it seems only to deepen her shame. In the first weeks after the accident she sleeps in bursts of an hour or two, waking with her heart racing as she hears the thud again. She avoids driving through that part of the city, then avoids driving altogether. Her late husband had always done most of the driving when he was alive, and after years of widowhood she had been proud of managing on her own. Now she takes cars to jobs and grips the door handle from the back seat, scanning every intersection. If a cyclist appears, her whole body goes rigid.

At work she remains outwardly composed. On set, photographers still call her effortless. She hates hearing that word. During one shoot for an activewear brand, a prop bicycle is rolled into frame and she feels the room tilt. She excuses herself to the restroom, where she sits in a locked stall pressing cold paper towels to her neck, furious with herself for being unable to calm down. She starts asking her agent for details before every booking—whether there will be street scenes, vehicles, anything involving motion. She turns down jobs she once would have accepted without hesitation. She tells people she is “slowing down selectively,” but privately she worries that her world is shrinking around one terrible second.

She thinks often about the injured woman, imagining pain, surgeries, months of dependence, the indignity of learning again how to move through the world. She has written apology letters she never sends, each one sounding to her either self-serving or inadequate. News stories about collisions hook her attention immediately. She reads them compulsively and then feels sick. At crosswalks she studies drivers’ faces with suspicion and contempt, then catches herself and remembers she was once the person behind the wheel.

Her family notices changes before she admits them. A daughter tells her she startles too easily. A grandson runs up behind her in the kitchen and she yells so sharply that he bursts into tears. After that she begins to fear her own reactions. She keeps the television low, avoids crowded restaurants, and positions herself near exits. When she does sleep, dreams come in fragments: brakes failing, a wheel spinning, a woman’s hand reaching up from the pavement. In the morning she often feels she has already lived through the worst part of the day.

What troubles her most is that the accident has altered the way she sees herself. Widowed life had already required a rebuilding of identity, but this feels different, corrosive. She had always considered herself careful, disciplined, professional. Now she carries a private conviction that she is dangerous when she stops paying attention, dangerous in the ordinary human ways everyone is sometimes careless. She becomes unforgiving toward herself in small matters—misplacing keys, missing an appointment time, forgetting to return a call—as if every lapse belongs to the same moral failure.

Even now, years later, she can be in hair and makeup before a campaign shoot, lights warming around her, and suddenly be back at the intersection: her phone glowing, the impossible bend of a leg, the helplessness of kneeling in the street while strangers take over. She keeps working. She arrives early, holds her posture, listens closely, and does what is asked of her. But underneath the polished stillness that has defined so much of her life, she is braced for impact.
